e-464.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
e-464.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\dfrac x 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac 1 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =3\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot 3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-465.knowledge_point: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
e-465.worked_solution:
If we let $u=6x+\dfrac \pi 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =\dfrac 1 6\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-466.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
e-466.worked_solution:
Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-467.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
e-467.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.$
e-467.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
content.worked_solution:
If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=4x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=3-9x, so dx=-du/9. Integrating gives -\frac{1}{9}\sin(3-9x)+C, which is option a.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=3-9x,$ then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3-9x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (-\frac{1}{9}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3-9x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Calculate ∫cos⁡(3−9x)dx.

a
−19sin⁡(3−9x)+C
b
19sin⁡(3−9x)+C
c
−13sin⁡(3−9x)+C
d
19cos⁡(3−9x)+C
e
−19cos⁡(3−9x)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If we let u=3−9x, then dudx=−9⟹dx=−19du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫cos⁡(3−9x)dx=∫cos⁡u⋅(−19du)=−19∫cos⁡udu=−19sin⁡u+C=−19sin⁡(3−9x)+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. By the chain rule, differentiating -\frac{1}{9}\sin(3-9x)+C gives cos(3-9x); option b gives its negative.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
content.worked_solution:
If we let $u=3-9x,$ then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3-9x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (-\frac{1}{9}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3-9x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

∫02cos⁡(πx4)dx=
Submit

decision.explanation: An antiderivative is (4/\pi)\sin(\pi x/4). Evaluating from 0 to 2 gives (4/\pi)(\sin(\pi/2)-\sin(0))=4/\pi.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{\pi x}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{4})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since the derivative of sec(10x) is 10sec(10x)tan(10x), the integral is \frac{1}{10}\sec(10x)+C, option a.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=10x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡(10x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(10x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{10}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sec}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sec}⁡(10x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,⟹\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+1)\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int ({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u+C \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x}{3}+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}

Question 8
?

Calculate the integral ∫(sec2⁡x+1)sec⁡xtan⁡xdx.

a
tan3⁡x3+sec⁡x+C
b
sec3⁡x3+sec⁡x+C
c
sec3⁡x3+C
d
tan3⁡x3+tan⁡x+C
e
sec2⁡x2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If we let u=sec⁡x, then

dudx=sec⁡xtan⁡x⟹sec⁡xtan⁡xdx=du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate:

∫(sec2⁡x+1)sec⁡xtan⁡xdx=∫(u2+1)du=u33+u+C=sec3⁡x3+sec⁡x+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
content.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,⟹\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+1)\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int ({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u+C \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x}{3}+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the integral ∫sec⁡(7x)tan⁡(7x)dx.

a
−17sec⁡(7x)+C
b
17sec⁡(7x)+C
c
7sec⁡(7x)+C
d
−7sec⁡(7x)+C

sec⁡(7x)+C

decision.explanation: The derivative of sec(7x) is 7sec(7x)tan(7x), so dividing by 7 gives the required antiderivative. Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=7x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡(7x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\operatorname{sec}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\operatorname{sec}⁡(7x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: An antiderivative is -(2/3)cot(3x). The integral equals -(2/3)(cot(π/2)-cot(π/3))=(2/3)(1/√3)=2√3/9, so option a is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=3x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /9$ | $\pi /6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /9}^{\pi /6}2{csc}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡u{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(0-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi }$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2\pi $ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(1-1) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡({x}^{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5)=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

So, differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $6$ | $5$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\cdot 24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{6}^{5} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡6) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{6}{5})\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=sin(y²), so du=2y cos(y²) dy. The integral becomes (1/2)∫du/u=(1/2)ln|sin(y²)|+C, which is option a.

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}))=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).
$$

So, let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}).$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\cdot (y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=2+csc(x), so du=−csc(x)cot(x) dx. The limits become 4 and 3, giving −∫₄³ du/u=ln(4)−ln(3).

after.name: Question 19
after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x),$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $3$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}\cdot (\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{4}^{3} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2|+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
content.worked_solution:
Let $u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2|+C\end{aligned}
$$
